nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Tropical sun drives growth of mangroves, forest plants and the algae that feed the bay.

nodes.name: Heavy rainfall
nodes.desc: The park is among the wettest in the country, with roughly 1,900 to 2,000 mm of rain a year, which feeds the humid forest and the bay.

nodes.name: Bay water and tides
nodes.desc: Salt water from San Lorenzo Bay floods the mangrove roots and carries the plankton and small fish the seabirds depend on.

nodes.name: Limestone karst soil
nodes.desc: Thin soils sit over limestone hills 200 to 300 m high, separated by sinkholes and riddled with caves.

nodes.name: Decomposers
nodes.desc: Fungi, bacteria and litter invertebrates break down fallen leaves and dead animals and return nutrients to the thin karst soil.

nodes.name: Red mangrove
nodes.desc: A salt-tolerant tree whose arching prop roots stand in brackish water. Its thickets give nesting and hunting habitat to fish, birds and crabs.

nodes.name: Bayrum tree
nodes.desc: A forest tree recorded in the park; GloBI records fruit bats feeding on it.

nodes.name: Spiral ginger
nodes.desc: A forest-understorey plant with showy flowers; GloBI records show birds such as the bananaquit feeding on it.

nodes.name: Phytoplankton
nodes.desc: Drifting algae in the bay that feed small schooling fish and other filter feeders.

nodes.name: Jamaican fruit bat
nodes.desc: A fruit eater that roosts in caves and other shelters and carries fruit away to roosts, which spreads seeds through the forest.

nodes.name: Hispaniolan hutia
nodes.desc: A threatened, nocturnal island rodent that mainly eats roots and fruits.

nodes.name: Bananaquit
nodes.desc: A small songbird that feeds on nectar and fruit; recorded feeding on spiral ginger in GloBI.

nodes.name: Forest arthropods
nodes.desc: Millipedes, beetles, crickets, ants and other invertebrates of the leaf litter and canopy, eating leaves and litter.

nodes.name: Small schooling fish
nodes.desc: Herring-like fish of warm bays that graze plankton. Pelicans elsewhere in the Caribbean rely on such fish.

nodes.name: Bark anole
nodes.desc: A small lizard on trunks and branches that hunts insects and other arthropods.

nodes.name: Robber frogs
nodes.desc: Small, direct-developing forest frogs that eat arthropods in leaf litter and are recorded in the park.

nodes.name: Hispaniolan solenodon
nodes.desc: An endangered nocturnal insectivore that probes soil and rotten logs for arthropods and also takes snails and small reptiles.

nodes.name: Turkey vulture
nodes.desc: The most-recorded bird in the area; it cleans up carrion along shores and clearings.

nodes.name: Great Egret
nodes.desc: A tall wader of mangrove shallows that spears fish and frogs.

nodes.name: Brown pelican
nodes.desc: A plunge-diving seabird that eats mainly fish and nests in mangroves and on islets.

nodes.name: Magnificent frigatebird
nodes.desc: Catches fish, squid and crustaceans at the surface and nests in colonies in mangrove cays such as the bird key of the bay.

nodes.name: Ridgway's hawk
nodes.desc: A critically endangered Hispaniolan raptor that takes mostly reptiles, plus birds, bats, rodents and frogs. The park holds one of its few surviving wild populations.

nodes.name: Stygian owl
nodes.desc: A night hunter of forest and caves, named by Wikipedia as a natural predator of the solenodon.
